quiz.question: What is the main principle of least privilege?
options: Give every process root access
Grant only the authority required for the task
Disable all permissions
Use one shared account for every service
quiz.explanation: The Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) dictates that any user, program, or process must possess only the minimum set of privileges, capabilities, and access rights essential to perform its intended function, minimizing damage in the event of compromise.

quiz.question: Which mechanism limits CPU or memory consumption by groups of processes?
options: Network namespaces alone
cgroups
File extensions
Secure Boot alone
quiz.explanation: Control Groups (cgroups, especially cgroup v2) provide resource accounting and hard/soft limits across CPU (cpu.max), memory (memory.max), process count (pids.max), and I/O bandwidth for collections of processes.

quiz.question: What does seccomp primarily help restrict?
options: System calls available to a process
Every network packet on the entire network
The firmware password
All filesystem permissions automatically
quiz.explanation: seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) uses BPF filters to intercept and restrict system calls at the kernel boundary, denying unneeded syscalls with EPERM, SIGSYS, or kill actions, dramatically reducing the exposed kernel attack surface.

quiz.question: What does Secure Boot help establish?
options: That all running applications are bug-free
A configured chain of trust during boot
That the machine can never be compromised
That all backups are recoverable
quiz.explanation: Secure Boot verifies cryptographic digital signatures on bootloaders, kernel images, and boot drivers against keys stored in firmware (UEFI db), ensuring only authorized and untampered code executes during the initial boot sequence.

quiz.question: Why should a security investigation preserve logs and timestamps?
options: To avoid documenting findings
To support a reliable event timeline and investigation
To prove every warning is malicious
To eliminate the need for backups
quiz.explanation: Preserving unmodified logs, metadata, and timestamps allows investigators to correlate events across authentication logs, system journals, and network connections, establishing a defensible chronological timeline of the incident.

quiz.question: What is the best approach to testing hardening changes?
options: Apply every change directly to a production host
Disable all security controls first
Use an authorized disposable environment, validate each change, and retain a recovery path
Assume a successful reboot proves security
quiz.explanation: Defensive engineering requires testing hardening controls in an isolated, disposable VM or staging environment with snapshot rollback capabilities, validating each change incrementally with evidence before production adoption.

theorySections.title: Users, Groups, Capabilities, and Least Privilege
paragraphs: Linux security begins with identity. The kernel associates every process with a User ID (UID), Group ID (GID), supplementary groups, and a set of cryptographic capabilities that dictate what privileged system calls and kernel operations the process is permitted to perform.
Configure process credentials, file permission bits, and kernel capabilities to evaluate privilege boundaries and attack exposure.

theorySections.title: Permissions, ACLs, Privilege Escalation, and Attack Surfaces
paragraphs: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) in Linux relies on 9 permission bits across owner, group, and others, augmented by special permission bits (setuid, setgid, sticky) and POSIX Access Control Lists (ACLs). Understanding where permission boundaries fail is the foundation of preventing privilege escalation.
When executed, the process assumes the effective user ID of the file's owner rather than the caller.
On directories, all newly created files inherit the parent directory's group ownership rather than the creator's primary GID.
On directories, users can only delete or rename files they own, even if the directory is world-writable (777).
Traditional Unix permissions only permit 1 owner and 1 group. POSIX ACLs allow granting explicit permissions to named users and groups without altering group memberships.

theorySections.title: Process Isolation, Namespaces, cgroups, and seccomp
paragraphs: Real container isolation is not a single feature; it is an orchestration of 4 independent kernel mechanisms: Namespaces (virtual views), cgroups (resource bounds), seccomp-bpf (system call filters), and LSMs (mandatory access control like AppArmor/SELinux).
Configure containment parameters and trigger malicious simulated payloads to verify sandbox defenses.

theorySections.title: Secure Boot, Kernel Integrity, and Patch Management
paragraphs: Security must be anchored in hardware. The Secure Boot trust chain guarantees that firmware, bootloaders, and kernel binaries have not been tampered with before execution begins.

theorySections.title: Resource Exhaustion and Denial-of-Service Defenses
paragraphs: Denial of Service (DoS) is not merely a network attack; it occurs whenever unbounded workloads exhaust CPU, RAM, file descriptors, process tables, or queue depth. Reliable operating systems implement explicit bounds and graceful load shedding.
Inject attack request traffic and observe how bounded queues, rate limiters, and CPU quotas protect availability.

The goal of system reliability is not to achieve infinite throughput under malicious floods. It is to enforce hard bounds, reject excess work with HTTP 429 / 503 errors, and guarantee that legitimate users and health-check monitoring retain system resources.

theorySections.title: Auditing, Logs, Incident Investigation, and Recovery
paragraphs: Security is incomplete without auditability and incident recovery. When an intrusion occurs, responders must stabilize the workload, preserve forensically sound evidence, establish an exact timeline, and execute verified restoration procedures.

theorySections.title: Threat Modeling for Local and Server Workloads
paragraphs: Threat modeling prevents security from being an arbitrary list of hardening commands. The STRIDE framework systematically identifies threats across Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege.
Select an application architecture to evaluate trust boundaries and defense-in-depth controls.

theorySections.title: Harden a Disposable Linux Environment
paragraphs: Execute an end-to-end security assessment across Phase A (Baseline Inventory), Phase B (Permissions Audit), Phase C (Controlled Hardening), Phase D (8-Point Checklist Validation), and Phase E (Assessment Report).
Production service sandbox with non-root UID, dropped capabilities, restricted syscalls, and resource ceilings.
